title: Royal Marines & Afghanistan to Personal Trainer — The Truth About This Industry
paragraphs: Hello everybody. Welcome back to PT Launch Lab and today I am joined by Jerome. How are we doing mate? Are we well? Thanks for coming over.

Um, so just at a glance, obvious we we try and look at everybody that comes in and just try and get an idea. So we've got some talk points. So former Royal Marines, uh, you've got a number of years experience in other sports, powerlifting. How long have you been in the industry now? Fitness >> started PT in 2019. >> 2019. >> Yeah. >> So was that how much of a gap between you leaving the military to get into a fitness injury?

Was it the first thing you did or did you find it? >> No, I left the military in 2014 and then I worked for the American government till 2018 in Afghanistan. Money, gun, golds, and drugs. >> So why transition into PT from there? Because I imagine the money was good. >> Yeah, the money was good, but I didn't want that life anymore. >> Yeah, >> you know. Yeah, >> you're living an abnormal life, but you think it's normal. It's not normal to do that anymore.

And and you you kind of leave the Marines and you think you know everything, but you just lived in this little protective bubble. Since I was a teenager, you know, I joined as a teenager that spent all my 20s there, most of my 30s. I'd never I'd never been to a coffee shop. I'd never been up for a meal. >> Normal life. >> Yeah. You don't understand what that is. >> Yeah.

And then you leave and you come. Well, I came to York to live above a sofa because I know where to go. You live on your sofa and you still think you're in the core, but everybody thinks this guy's got something wrong with them, but you're just trying to still be who you think you should be. >> So, I mean, I've always been interested in people leaving the mil, not necessarily just being in there, but leaving. >> Yeah. How long did it take you to reaclimate to normal life or what we consider normal life to be present in that? >> I would say I'm still doing that now. >> Yeah, I'd say I'm a lot better. I'd go with eight years ago I met my misses who were currently married and she proper saved me.

She's screwed my way. I haven't drunk alcohol for coming on nine years now. to stop that. >> Fantastic. I really like >> um God dashound. >> Yeah, >> a dog will help you. >> Yeah, >> but it's that Peter Pan life and I wrote a little I wrote I like to write so I wrote this PDF just sits on my laptop and I call it the Netherland theory and when you're in the military or the core, you live the Peter Pan life. You know, you're chasing Tinker Bells around Plymouth, you're going to pubs, you're eating buffet, it's just a game. And then you go on tour, you do your thing on tour, you come back and it's just this reconditioning of the cycle.

Go chase Captain Hook, come back, chase Tinkerbell. And then when you leave that bubble and Peter has to come back to the reality of life, he doesn't really know what to do. And the people you knew at that time, they either stay or go or they go back to where they come from, which is some random place in Britain or Scotland usually, and you just left on your own. So when you moved into fitness then did it sort of fill some of those gaps that you felt were missing in terms of because I imagine you are a very disciplined person in a lot of ways and I can't imagine there were many jobs out there that were going to fulfill that need. So is that why you chose fitness? >> I'm going to be completely honest with you.

When you're a boot neck, all you know is fizz fighting. >> Yeah. >> Right. >> You got three options. >> I chose fizz. Yeah. You know what I mean? I chose fizz and I quickly realized >> that nobody wants to join the Raw Marines and they don't want to be trained like it. >> Yeah. >> And then you're like, I don't even have a business. This isn't even a business.

I'm just trying to give people a workout. And I'll go into like the evolution of where I'm at now to where I began because I always look back on this sliding scale of the ecosystem of where we sit as trainers, coaches, educators, and then you've got your top 1% you talked about that you know might be training Manchester United or leaders. At the beginning I was just given workouts. I was like my first ever client, she worked as the house. She was in charge of the cake.

It's like this with it. They basically roll out food that they want to put into the bigger shops. Yeah. I absolutely thrashed her and nothing changed. And then she was like, I don't know what this is.

And I was like, I don't know what this is either, so I'm not going to lie to you. Yeah. And then you just have to try and figure that out. And it wasn't actually till I met the misses and she was like, you could be a lot better. you just need to look at what it is you want to do. And she pushed me into the idea that I could be better and I could go and get education.
And so I just started from that moment. Uh going to whoever was at the top, expediate that process. Same as the military. If you can join the raw marines or the partial regiment, join them. Why not?

So apply that to, you know, who's got to be the formal guy in that field that I need education from. And that's where I started. >> Do you think the obviously we are an education company how important is education when it comes to a professional service like this? I think you have the two sides of the coin. I think you need the education to start in this in the industry. You need to understand what this is.

You know, I think the more you develop, you need more education because you're going to push into what it is that you want to do more of. But experience on the floor and training lots of different people and understanding what that looks like, will it push you forward? It's um it's a really interesting topic because a lot of the time then we're speaking to brand new people that are coming in to learn. What they want to do is they want to understand everything that's in that textbook. And don't get me wrong, if that is something you're into, fantastic. Absorb it all. But the reality is, and I treat it a lot like passing your test and driving.

You can do the theory side, you can smash that, you can pass your test with flying colors, but you don't know how to drive. You need to get out there and do stuff. And I think when it comes into the fitness industry, you obviously I know that you've got a hot take on this. But the industry today, I feel like, has taken a couple of backst steps in this manner because we're too now relying on social media as a face. I think AI people are using it in a way that replaces their train of thought.

They're trying to replace their effort level and we're leaving out the the actual emotional side to training people because again, we can train people all day and give them programs and give them nutrition. But if you give that to 100 people, less than 20 probably follow through with it. >> Yeah. >> Because they don't understand why. >> Yeah. People forget it's called personal training. >> Yeah. That's exactly what it is. It's um so when you started pushing yourself towards this then and the evolution, what did what have you learned in your time of being a personal trainer or some lessons that you had during that process? biggest lessons are probably humility >> because you learn one thing, you keep applying it, but it doesn't mean you know everything and not one thing lasts forever and not one thing works for everybody.

I think you have to be true to yourself as well. You shouldn't get lost up in the the light box or the black mirror because that'll only reflect on what it is that that wants to show you. >> Explain that to me then. So, what do you mean by these two concepts? I know you you were going to choose one. So, what do you mean by these concepts?

The light box and the black mirror. >> Oh, that's the phone, isn't it? So, >> yeah. >> You know, essentially, it's just the light box. It's just a box of light. Doesn't really mean anything. It's just showing you pictures of what it is you think your own reality is. >> Yeah. >> And the Black Mirror is a program that was on BBC 2, I believe, or Channel 4.

Yeah. It was like a paradigm universe of what people were seeing when they were living. And there's this idea where you look on social media, any of the platforms really, and it'll just reflect on what you want to see. And I think that's become detrimental to a lot of things. It's a powerful tool, don't get me wrong. >> Yeah, >> it's very powerful.

It has it has so many benefits but it can also come it's like with anything you know if you overtake medication it's not medication anymore it becomes something that's harmful and you know even to this day ever since having my daughter for instance I had to really try and understand a lot more about how much I use my phone cuz you know when you're self-employed you're always working your brain's always working and I noticed it without even knowing I was looking at my phone for updates Even notifications, they weren't mattering to me anymore. I was checking for notifications and you're seeking the next step, the next approval, the next buzz. And you realize you separate yourself from the real world. >> Yeah. >> You know, um, and I think everyone gets hooked on that. I think no one is 100% clean from that. I don't think you can be.

It's not the way the world works now. But especially like with how you explained it, the the the light box theories, we can put it down at any time and whatever's on there is what we chose to see and what the algorithm tells you they want to see. >> And so you were you talking a little bit about how you worked with your clients and tried to get them to realize some of these negative aspects of that. >> Yeah. >> What was your idea? How did you run that? Um, what I used to do was, and I still do now, but I do it through a a spreadsheet, is I build a a wheel and we have the six pillars that hold up the wheel essentially. And if you can't fill those six pillars of who you are and what it is that you want, then you have something missing in your life or you have something missing that in your purpose because we all have passion.

We all have purpose, but without that, you're not able to take them forward because like I said to you in the beginning is like the gym is just a bunch of stuff in a room. It's plastic and metal and it's how you apply what it is you want to do with it to get the result. But sometimes the result is bigger than we are just going to do x amount of sets and reps. The resulting in them having a stronger purpose for what it is that they want is what gives them that drive. So, usually people will say say things like family, children, but they'll lack the ability to fill all six gaps.

They'll put the things they class as most important to them first, and then they lack usually the ability to say themselves. >> Yeah. What does it do for you? This room with stuff in it. >> The gym. >> Do you know what? In the beginning when I was younger, I just love going to the gym, >> you know, like the feeling of like working out, you feel great, and then you get a bit older and a couple years older and you get to like mid-4s. And I'll be honest, I don't have that pure passion to go in the gym all of the time.

But I need the idea that I need a structure and a and a routine. Otherwise, what am I going to do? Do you feel like that is going to be the case for I feel like most personal trainers have this opinion unless you are someone who's probably might be in a sport competing against something. Everyone asked me this and everyone assumes it's about a personal trainer because you work in a gym because you are always around. It's like you've always got time to work out like it's actually the biggest crux ever because you spend enough time there you don't want to be there anymore.

Um so I I get the exact feeling. I think no one really considers that aspect is when you turn your playing to work. >> Yeah. >> It doesn't become as fun and you're doing it for like you say you're you understand the benefits. So then you actually put yourself in the position of a like almost a beginner client in a way. You're teaching the value of it first and you know the value you just have to practice it. And uh we actually had this interesting conversation about if the trainer isn't practicing what they preach, >> should they be practicing?

I've met some amazing trainers, coaches, and educators that don't really train. So I don't think you need to. Not if you not if you've implemented that over a large space of your time. Do you need to train five days a week? you know, could you train once or twice? Yes.

But the knowledge that he can give you, and that's all he's really bothered about now is passing on knowledge. >> Yeah.

Yeah. >> Give one, pass it on. >> He's in his 50s. Does he still need to train any? Does he still want to? >> He's been doing it since he was 15. >> But do you agree that you have got to have walked the walk at some point? >> Yeah, I think you have to have walked the walk. I think you can't tell somebody how to squat 250 if you haven't done yourself. >> Yeah, exactly. Yeah, it's um Yeah, I agree with that.

I'm not about six weeks. I'm not about eight weeks. And there's nothing wrong with that. People are doing that. That's cool, man.

That's the thing. It's not my thing. So you have that return to play protocol and I get a lot of that as well and then they stay because the process is interactive where everything is layered because it has to be a layering process. You know, like we talked about is complexity upon complexity because the human is the most complex organism in the world.

But then there's the layers, isn't there? those somebody given workouts, there's a personal trainer, there's a coach, there's an educator, and then there's the top 2%. >> Yeah.
